other-interests-80993f7191.headline: Too hot to sleep? How heatwaves at night affect our health
other-interests-80993f7191.fulltext:
Global warming isn’t just about heat during the day. Nights are also getting hotter1–3. In May, Delhi recorded an overnight minimum temperature of 32.4 °C, and other parts of India remained 3–5 °C above normal after dark. As Western Europe experienced its hottest June on record, France registered a record overnight low of 22 °C, and East Saxony, Germany, sweltered at a historic 29.4 °C. In July, record night-time warmth exceeding 27 °C added to the mugginess of cities on the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
Heat affects people’s sleep (see ‘Global sleep deficit’). Two-thirds of respondents to a UK survey said they struggled to sleep during the June heatwave, with almost half losing at least three hours of sleep each night (see go.nature.com/5rcv6y). An analysis of more than 1,300 cities found that, during 2020–25, each resident lost nearly 56 hours of sleep, on average, each year owing to night-time heat4.
The consequences go beyond lost sleep. Across 28 East Asian cities, intense heatwaves at night were associated with a 3% increase in deaths (excluding those from injuries and other external causes)3. In Hong Kong, long, hot nights — around 30 °C for 12 hours — were linked to a 3.1% rise in emergency hospital admissions, reaching 5.3% among older and poorer people2.
But scientists don’t fully understand how hot nights affect health and sleep. To get the full picture, measuring temperatures alone is insufficient; people’s physiological responses to heat must also be studied. Here’s what is needed to better understand the link and manage night-time heat.
At night, people are biologically programmed for recovery
Sleep is crucial for health because it enables our bodies and brains to recover from daily strains. Regulated by our circadian system, our levels of physiological arousal and cardiovascular activity fall when we sleep. Our nervous system, metabolism and immune system are rebalanced. Different stages of sleep help us to consolidate memories and support mechanisms of cognitive and emotional control5.
To save lives in heatwaves, focus on how human bodies work
As we wind down and prepare for sleep, our core body temperature drops, initiating restorative processes. Peripheral blood vessels dilate and transfer heat from the centre of the body to the skin and extremities. But when the temperature in the bedroom is too high, and especially when it is humid, the body’s cooling is impaired — and sleep quality suffers5.
When people are awake, they can drink water, move around, open windows, use fans or seek cooler spaces to help restore thermal balance. When they are asleep, however, their ability to take actions to control body temperature is limited. Thus, it is harder to get to sleep and stay asleep in a hot room6.
Night-time heat can also strain the body. The heart pumps more blood to the skin to shed internal heat, which elevates the heart rate. Sustained sweating can lead to dehydration. These physical demands can be particularly taxing for older adults and people with weak cardiovascular systems.
In hot weather, all these disruptions combine to increase health risks. Heat exposure increases physiological arousal, as reflected in an elevated heart rate and increased sweating. Waking up to drink water or change position interrupts the restorative sequence of sleep stages. Broken sleep can in turn weaken cardiovascular, metabolic, immune, cognitive and emotional recovery, contributing to fatigue, impaired attention and poor regulation of physiological processes the next day5,7,8.
Medical researchers understand the parts of these processes. But they haven’t quantified them adequately and fully determined how they’re linked in a vicious circle. Climate change means that many more people will be exposed to hot nights more often. As we all adapt, researchers and policymakers must ask not just how hot the day will be, but whether the night will allow people to cool down, sleep and recover (see ‘Night-time heat: five research priorities’).
Heat health risks need to be tracked
Conventional night-time heat metrics based on meteorological anomalies are useful for tracking climate trends. For example, a tropical night is often defined as one in which the outdoor air temperature stays above 20 °C — or higher in some regions, such as 25 °C in South Korea. Indices of consecutive hot nights count runs of two or more nights exceeding a temperature threshold1.
But these data are inadequate for medical purposes. They fail to capture the temperature indoors and the exact timing and duration of heat exposure paired with sleep quality through the night, for instance. We argue that researchers and policymakers should instead assess night-time risk in terms of an imbalance between the thermal load someone experiences and their body’s capacity to recover.
Time to give hydration breaks the red card? What science says about keeping cool
Thermal load can be quantified as the number of hours during which bedroom conditions exceed a health-relevant temperature threshold during the sleeping period, and participants’ recovery can be measured in several ways.
Cost-effective sensors can be used to record air temperature and humidity every few minutes8,9. In field studies, these sensors could be placed in bedrooms, and participants could wear devices on the wrist that record sleep timing, sleep continuity, movement, skin temperature, heart rate and heart-rate variability8,9. Measuring morning blood pressure, fatigue, sleepiness and attention can indicate whether recovery was completed overnight.
Small samples could be used to validate larger studies through detailed monitoring of body core temperature and sleep stages, using sensors and electrodes applied to the skin5,8. With informed consent, participants’ records could be linked to their health-care data.
Such methods are already technically feasible and have been used to investigate the effects of air quality on sleep10 — uncovering an association between warmer, poorly ventilated bedrooms and poorer sleep, particularly among older adults8,9. A platform called HeatSuite has demonstrated the feasibility of integrating data from environmental sensors with those from wearable devices, such as blood-pressure and temperature measurements, in older adults11.
These approaches should now be extended to cohorts monitored before, during and after hot nights. Repeated observations are essential to test whether incomplete overnight recovery leaves residual physiological strain for days. Environmental, sleep and physiological measures should be collected for several weeks, supplemented by short daily surveys of symptoms, medication and cooling behaviours.
Such studies could establish the degree to which incomplete recovery contributes to increased mortality and hospital admissions during hot nights2,3. They could explore the effects of long or repeated moderately hot nights, and test whether real-time indoor temperature is more relevant than is an outdoor minimum.

other-interests-f50bc2db63.headline: Britain’s only desalination plant remains idle during drought
other-interests-f50bc2db63.fulltext:
Water levels on the river Thames in London have dropped low enough to allow the production of drinking water from mainland Britain’s only desalination plant – but it is currently out of service.
The £250 million Thames Gateway desalination plant in Beckton, east London, opened in 2010 and remains mainland Britain’s only large-scale desalination plant. It was designed to provide additional drinking water to the capital during times of severe drought by turning brackish water from the Thames into potable water.
But despite the UK recording its driest July since records began in 1836 and suffering what government officials have described as an “exceptionally serious” drought, the plant has not been used at all this year.
Advertisement
Under Thames Water’s drought plan, the firm is allowed to start using its desalination plant if a drought is declared and if water flow rates in the Thames drop below 3000 megalitres per day (Ml/d).
A drought was declared in England on 29 July 2026, and data obtained by New Scientist suggests water flow rates at Teddington in south-west London, the lowest point of the freshwater Thames, have been well below the 3000 Ml/d mark for weeks.
In fact, the current rates are around 220 Ml/d, below even the target river flow threshold for Teddington of 300 Ml/d agreed by Thames Water and the Environment Agency during the current drought. Normally, the target flow rate for the river is 800 Ml/d, to protect the river’s ecology and surrounding environment from over-abstraction by Thames Water.
Under normal circumstances, the current situation would allow Thames Water to start producing drinking water from the Beckton plant, to relieve pressure on other water sources. The Thames Gateway plant is capable of providing up to 100 Ml/d of water, about 4 per cent of the daily volume of drinking water supplied by Thames Water.
But the desalination plant has been beset with technical problems and is currently out of supply, according to Thames Water. Its 2027 draft drought plan published earlier this year reports that work is under way to replace damaged equipment, including the plant’s membranes, which act as filters for fresh water.
The plant has only ever run five times, reporting last year revealed, delivering the equivalent of seven days’ worth of drinking water supplies to London. It has not been used at all this year, despite the worsening drought. Thames Water’s drought plan suggests the plant would take four to six weeks to ramp up to full capacity.
A spokesperson for Thames Water said the firm was working to ready the plant for operations later this year. They said in a statement: “Preparations are under way at the Thames Gateway Water Treatment Works in Beckton East London so it can be brought online by the end of the year, if needed, to help support reservoir recovery over the winter. Any decision to use the desalination plant will depend on weather conditions, demand, and reservoir levels in the coming weeks.”
Data released by the Environment Agency this month confirmed that July 2026 was the driest July for the Thames area since records began in 1871, with the region receiving just 1 millimetre of rainfall for the entire month. Parts of the river Thames are suffering exceptionally low flows, which can lead to low oxygen levels and deteriorating river health.
The problems at the Beckton desalination plant come as other water companies look to build desalination plants across England, in a bid to shore up water supplies as climate change brings more frequent and intense droughts to the country.
Anglian Water is developing plans for two plants in Norfolk and Lincolnshire, using seawater from the North Sea. Meanwhile, South West Water is also drawing up plans for a desalination plant in Par, Cornwall, to help the county cope with the increased water demands during the busy summer months.

other-interests-c06176a6fc.headline: Only a few hundred Timor green pigeons may remain. There is still time to save them
other-interests-c06176a6fc.fulltext:
Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries.
On April 20, on the south coast of Timor-Leste, Jafet Potenzo Lopes saw three green pigeons. He had not seen the species for years. The birds were Timor green pigeons, and the site, in Manatuto municipality, had no previous record of them. With the species nearing extinction, finding three birds in a new place was encouraging.
The latest estimates suggest how few remain. A study published this year in Oryx, drawing on more than 1,400 days of field surveys between 2002 and 2025, estimates the global population at 100-500 birds across eight sites. The true number may be near the lower end of that range. Only Nino Konis Santana National Park in eastern Timor-Leste is thought to hold more than 50 birds. The researchers recommend changing the status of the Timor green pigeon (Treron psittaceus) on the IUCN Red List from endangered to critically endangered, reports contributor Timothy Mihocik for Mongabay.
In Indonesia, where many older records came from West Timor and nearby islands, the pigeon may already be functionally extinct. Most of the remaining birds are in Timor-Leste, where hunting continues even in protected areas.
Timor green pigeons gather at fruiting trees and are unusually vulnerable: After one bird is shot, others may stay in the canopy. Forest conversion has also reduced their habitat. More than 80% of known records come from protected areas, yet researchers say those areas lack the funding and staff needed to control hunting effectively.
The danger has been recognized for years. The species has been classed as endangered since 2000, while dedicated recovery work, regular monitoring and sustained investment have remained limited. The Timor green pigeon was not among the initial 100 species selected by the Phoenix Species Project, a $200 million initiative by Re:wild and the Bezos Earth Fund to support recovery of some of the world’s most threatened species.
Researchers say the pigeon can still be saved. They recommend more surveys, monitoring of its main population every three to five years, a national action plan and work with hunters and local communities to reduce hunting. Timor-Leste already protects the species under national law and customary systems protect some of the forests where it survives. Researchers have also suggested involving former hunters in surveys and conservation work.
The three birds found in Manatuto do little to change the species’ overall position. They do show that some birds remain in places where they had not previously been recorded. With perhaps only a few hundred Timor green pigeons left, the margin is narrow. The steps needed to improve their chances are already known.

opportunities-9cce553633.headline: UK Chevening Scholarship 2027-28 Applications Open: Check Eligibility, Deadline and Key Details
opportunities-9cce553633.fulltext:
Applications for the UK government’s prestigious Chevening Scholarship 2027-28 are now open, offering Indian students and professionals an opportunity to pursue a fully funded one-year taught master’s degree at eligible universities across the United Kingdom. The scholarship is supported by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) and partner organisations and is designed to develop future leaders who can contribute to positive change in their home countries. For ambitious professionals looking to gain international academic exposure while strengthening their leadership and professional networks, the opening of the 2027-28 cycle provides an important opportunity. However, applicants will need to meet the prescribed eligibility conditions and submit their applications before the deadline.
Chevening Applications Open for 2027-28
The Chevening programme offers selected scholars the opportunity to study a one-year taught master’s course in the UK. Beyond academic learning, the programme places considerable emphasis on leadership, networking and long-term impact.
The scholarship is intended for individuals who demonstrate strong leadership potential, professional experience and the ability to contribute meaningfully to their communities and countries. Scholars also become part of an international alumni network that continues beyond their time in the UK.
For Indian applicants, the current application cycle will remain open until 6th October 2026 at 11:00 UTC, which is 4:30 pm IST. Candidates should complete the application well before the closing time because the online system will not accept submissions after the deadline.
Important Points for Applicants
Candidates planning to apply should keep the following details in mind:
- Applications for the 2027-28 Chevening cycle are currently open
- The application deadline is 6th October 2026 at 11:00 UTC
- Indian applicants should note the corresponding deadline of 4:30 pm IST
- The scholarship supports a one-year taught master’s programme in the UK
- Applicants must demonstrate leadership potential and professional experience
- Candidates must meet Chevening’s academic and work-experience requirements
- Applicants must select three eligible UK university courses
Who Can Apply for the Scholarship?
The Chevening selection process is aimed at candidates with a combination of academic preparation, professional experience, leadership potential and clear future ambitions.
According to the official eligibility criteria, applicants must have completed an undergraduate degree that qualifies them for entry to a UK master’s programme. Their undergraduate studies must have been completed at least two years before the application deadline.
Applicants must also have at least two years of work experience, equivalent to 2,800 hours, acquired after completing their undergraduate degree. This requirement means that the scholarship is particularly relevant to working professionals and graduates who have already developed experience in their chosen fields.
Candidates must also commit to returning to their home country for at least two years after completing the scholarship. This reflects the programme’s wider objective of developing professionals who can use their knowledge and networks to contribute to their countries after their UK studies.
Course Selection Is an Important Step
Choosing the right programme is another important part of the application. Applicants must select three eligible UK university courses as part of their Chevening application.
The selected courses must meet the programme’s eligibility conditions. Chevening states that eligible courses must be UK-based, full-time, begin in the autumn term and lead to a taught master’s qualification. Applicants must also apply separately to the universities offering their chosen courses, as submitting a Chevening application does not itself constitute a university admission application.
This makes early research particularly important. Candidates should examine course structures, entry requirements, academic content and career relevance before finalising their choices.
What Makes Chevening Different?
The value of the programme extends beyond financial support for postgraduate education. Chevening is structured around leadership development, professional networking and international engagement.
Scholars spend a year studying in the UK while interacting with people from different professional and cultural backgrounds. These experiences can help candidates develop broader perspectives and establish networks that may support their future careers.
The programme’s alumni network is another important component. Chevening currently highlights a community of more than 60,000 alumni, demonstrating the global scale of the network available to scholars after graduation.
For candidates considering a fully funded master’s degree, this combination of financial support, academic experience and international networking makes the scholarship particularly significant.
Selection Goes Beyond Academic Performance
Applicants should not assume that strong academic qualifications alone will guarantee selection. The programme evaluates candidates on a broader set of qualities, including leadership, networking ability, career plans and potential to create positive change.
This means applicants should present a clear connection between their academic goals, professional experience and long-term ambitions. Their application should demonstrate not only what they hope to gain from studying in the UK but also how they intend to use that experience afterwards.
The emphasis on future impact is central to Chevening’s purpose. The programme seeks individuals who can translate international education and professional networks into meaningful contributions in their home countries.
Why Indian Applicants Should Plan Early
With the deadline approaching in October, prospective Indian applicants should avoid leaving the application until the final days. Preparing a strong application requires time, particularly when candidates need to research eligible courses, prepare written responses, and gather the necessary information.
Applicants should first confirm that they meet every eligibility condition. They should then identify suitable courses and examine the requirements of each university separately.
EducationToday’s coverage of international education opportunities continues to highlight how scholarships can make global postgraduate education more accessible to ambitious Indian professionals. The Chevening programme stands out because it combines study with leadership development and an extensive international network.
Application Timeline and What Happens Next
Once applications close on 6th October 2026, submissions will undergo eligibility checks and the selection process will progress through subsequent stages. Chevening’s official timeline states that applications are sifted against eligibility criteria from October 2026, with shortlisted candidates progressing towards interviews. Successful candidates will ultimately need to secure an unconditional offer from at least one eligible UK university course. For the 2027-28 cycle, the deadline for receiving and submitting at least one unconditional offer is 8th July 2027 at 17:00 BST. Studies are scheduled to begin in September or October 2027.
An Opportunity for Future Global Leaders
The opening of the Chevening Scholarship 2027-28 applications allows Indian graduates and professionals to pursue advanced education in the UK while developing international networks and leadership capabilities.
Candidates should approach the application as more than a request for financial support. A successful application needs to communicate a clear professional journey, credible leadership experience and a well-defined vision for the future.
With applications open until 6th October 2026, prospective scholars have time to research their options, understand the eligibility requirements and prepare a considered application. For those who meet the criteria and have a clear ambition to create impact after their studies, the programme could become an important step towards a globally connected academic and professional career.

Call for Applications: Gordon R. Sullivan Climate and Ecological Security Fellowship 2026–2027
The Center for Climate and Security (CCS), an initiative of the Council on Strategic Risks, has opened applications for the 2026–2027 Gordon R. Sullivan Climate and Ecological Security Fellowship. The professional development programme is designed for emerging professionals working at the intersection of climate change, environmental issues, and national or international security.
Named in honour of General Gordon Sullivan, a former U.S. Army leader and early advocate for integrating climate and environmental considerations into national security planning, the fellowship seeks to cultivate the next generation of public servants and professionals working on climate-security challenges.
The unpaid, part-time fellowship will run from October 2026 through July 2027, combining virtual learning, expert engagement, structured discussions, and independent work.
About the Sullivan Fellowship
The fellowship is a professional development programme that provides participants with an opportunity to deepen their understanding of the relationship between climate change, ecological challenges, and security.
Fellows will participate in monthly two-hour virtual sessions featuring guest speakers, small-group activities, discussions, assigned readings, and other curriculum-based activities.
The programme will examine a broad range of emerging climate-security issues, including:
- Food and water security
- Climate-related migration
- Climate adaptation and resilience
- The role of militaries and intelligence services
- Disinformation and democracy
- The global energy transition
- Technology and artificial intelligence
- Strategic competition
- Climate intervention and geoengineering
Through these sessions, fellows will have opportunities to engage with experts and peers while developing knowledge relevant to careers in public service, climate policy, environmental security, and national or international security.
Who Is Eligible?
The fellowship has specific eligibility requirements. Applicants must:
- Be based in the United States.
- Have between one and five years of post-undergraduate professional experience in climate change, environmental issues, and/or national or international security.
- Demonstrate a strong and established interest in pursuing a career connected to the intersection of these fields.
- Commit to participating actively in the fellowship programme.
Applicants should therefore have relevant professional experience rather than relying solely on undergraduate academic experience.
Attendance Requirements
Successful fellows are expected to make a substantial commitment to the programme. To use the credential “2026–2027 Sullivan Fellow” after completing the programme, participants must attend and actively participate in at least seven fellowship sessions.
Sessions are scheduled virtually on the third Thursday of each month, from 6:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. Eastern Time, between October 2026 and July 2027.
The scheduled dates are:
- October 15, 2026
- November 19, 2026
- December 17, 2026
- January 21, 2027
- February 18, 2027
- March 18, 2027
- April 15, 2027
- May 20, 2027
- June 17, 2027
- July 15, 2027
Applicants should ensure that their professional and personal commitments allow them to participate consistently throughout the programme.
Special Consideration for Public Service Professionals
The organisers have indicated that special consideration will be given to applicants whose public service careers have been affected by U.S. federal job cuts, budget reductions, and/or policy changes since 2025.
This consideration recognises the impact that recent changes in public-sector employment and policy environments may have had on professionals working in climate, environmental, and security-related fields.
Application Requirements
The application process is designed to be concise. Applicants are required to complete an online application form containing:
- A one-page resume
- Brief written responses to three application questions
The written responses provide applicants with an opportunity to demonstrate their professional background, interests, career aspirations, and understanding of climate and ecological security issues.
Applicants should ensure that their resume clearly communicates relevant professional experience and that their written responses demonstrate a focused interest in the climate-security field.
Application Deadline
Applications are being reviewed on a rolling basis, meaning applicants are encouraged to apply before the final deadline rather than waiting until the end of the application period.
The application period closes at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on September 14, 2026.
Programme Benefits
Although the Sullivan Fellowship is unpaid, it offers professional development opportunities for individuals seeking to strengthen their expertise and networks in climate and ecological security.
Participants will gain exposure to:
- Experienced climate and security practitioners
- Specialist guest speakers
- Peer discussions and collaborative activities
- Current climate-security research and policy debates
- Emerging issues affecting national and international security
- Perspectives on climate adaptation, resilience, technology, and strategic competition
The programme can therefore provide a structured environment for early-career professionals to expand their knowledge and develop relationships within the climate-security community.
How to Apply
Eligible applicants should complete the official online application form and submit the required resume and written responses before the September 14, 2026 deadline.
The Gordon R. Sullivan Climate and Ecological Security Fellowship 2026–2027 represents an opportunity for U.S.-based early-career professionals to develop specialised knowledge at the intersection of climate change, ecological challenges, and security while engaging with experts and peers throughout a 10-month professional development programme.
